why: Personal data protection is part of almost every GRC role in Europe, and many compliance analyst and DPO assistant offers ask for GDPR (RGPD in French) by name. Recruiters expect you to know the principles and lawful bases, to keep a record of processing, to judge when an impact assessment is needed, to handle a rights request and a data breach on time, and to review a processor or a transfer outside the EU.
outcome: explain the scope and key terms of the GDPR, apply the principles and choose a lawful basis, handle data subject rights within the deadlines, keep the record of processing activities and set retention periods, decide when a DPIA is required and carry one out, check a processor contract and a transfer outside the EU, and manage a personal data breach from detection to notification within 72 hours.

lessons.title: Scope and key terms
text: The General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679, applied since 25 May 2018, protects people when their personal data is used. As a regulation, it applies directly in every EU country, with some national details: in France, the Loi Informatique et Libertés completes it and the CNIL is the supervisory authority. It applies to organisations established in the EU, and also to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour.

Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable living person: a name, an e-mail address, an ID number, an IP address, location data, a photo, a voice recording, or a combination of details that makes someone identifiable. Pseudonymised data, where names are replaced by codes but a key exists somewhere, is still personal data. Truly anonymous data, where nobody can identify the person any more by reasonable means, is outside the GDPR.

Processing means any operation on personal data: collecting, recording, storing, consulting, using, sharing, combining, deleting. The controller decides why and how the data is processed and carries the main responsibility, for example an employer for its payroll. The processor processes data on behalf of the controller and following its instructions, for example the payroll software provider. When two organisations decide together, they are joint controllers and must agree on who does what.

Two principles run through the whole regulation. Accountability: the controller must not only comply but be able to demonstrate compliance, with documents, records and decisions. Risk-based approach: the stronger the risk for people’s rights and freedoms, the stronger the measures, which is why some obligations, such as impact assessments, depend on the risk.

The stakes are high. Supervisory authorities can order changes, ban processing and impose fines of up to 20 million euros or 4 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the most serious infringements such as breaching the principles or people’s rights; and up to 10 million euros or 2 % for others, such as failing to keep records or to notify a breach. People can also complain and claim compensation.
points: GDPR (EU) 2016/679, applied since 25 May 2018; in France completed by the Loi Informatique et Libertés, supervised by the CNIL.
Personal data: any information about an identifiable living person; pseudonymised data is still personal data.
Controller decides why and how; processor acts on its instructions; joint controllers decide together.
Accountability: comply and be able to prove it.
Fines up to 20 M€ or 4 % of worldwide turnover (whichever is higher), or 10 M€ / 2 % for other infringements.

lessons.title: Principles and lawful bases
text: Article 5 sets seven principles. Lawfulness, fairness and transparency: a legal basis, no hidden use, clear information. Purpose limitation: collect for specified, explicit purposes and do not reuse the data for incompatible ones. Data minimisation: only the data that is adequate, relevant and necessary. Accuracy: keep it correct and up to date. Storage limitation: keep it in identifiable form no longer than necessary. Integrity and confidentiality: appropriate security. And accountability, which ties them together.

Every processing needs one of six lawful bases (article 6), chosen before it starts and recorded. Consent: freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, as easy to withdraw as to give, for example a newsletter tick box that is not pre-ticked. Contract: necessary to perform a contract with the person, such as delivering an order. Legal obligation: required by law, such as keeping invoices or declaring salaries. Vital interests: to protect someone’s life. Public task: for public authorities. Legitimate interests: the organisation’s interest, when it is not overridden by the person’s rights, after a balancing test, for example fraud prevention.

Consent is not always the best basis. In employment, consent is rarely free because of the imbalance of power, so payroll relies on contract and legal obligation. Using consent where another basis applies also creates trouble when people withdraw it. Choose the basis that matches reality, and do not switch bases afterwards.

Special categories of data (article 9) are prohibited in principle unless an exception applies: data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data used to identify someone, health data, and data on sex life or sexual orientation. Exceptions include explicit consent, obligations of employment law, health care and some public interest cases. Data on criminal convictions (article 10) is also strictly limited.

In practice the principles turn into questions you ask about every new project: why do we need this data, which basis applies, could we use less, how long do we keep it, who can access it, and how do we tell people? Asking them early is what privacy by design means.
points: Seven principles: lawfulness-fairness-transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity-confidentiality, accountability.
Six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests.
Consent: free, specific, informed, unambiguous, easy to withdraw; rarely valid in employment.
Special categories (health, biometrics for identification, religion, union membership…) prohibited unless an article 9 exception applies.
Choose and record the basis before processing; do not switch later.

Delivering online orders                 Contract                  Address, phone for the carrier
Keeping invoices 10 years                Legal obligation          French commercial and tax law
Marketing newsletter                     Consent                   Box not pre-ticked, unsubscribe link
Fraud scoring of payments                Legitimate interests      Balancing test documented
Sick leave certificates (HR)             Legal obligation + art. 9 Employment law exception

lessons.title: People’s rights and transparency
text: People must be told how their data is used, at the time of collection (article 13) or within a month when the data comes from elsewhere (article 14). The privacy notice gives the controller’s identity and contact, the DPO’s contact if there is one, the purposes and lawful bases, the recipients, transfers outside the EU, retention periods, the person’s rights, the right to complain to the supervisory authority, and whether providing the data is required. It must be concise, clear and easy to find, in plain language.

The GDPR gives people several rights. Access (article 15): obtain a copy of their data and information about its use. Rectification (16): correct inaccurate data. Erasure, the “right to be forgotten” (17): deletion in defined cases, for example when the data is no longer needed or consent is withdrawn, but not when a legal obligation requires keeping it. Restriction (18): freeze the use while a dispute is checked. Portability (20): receive data they provided in a reusable format, when processing is based on consent or contract and automated. Objection (21): object to processing based on legitimate interests or public task, and always to direct marketing. And article 22 protects against decisions based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects.

Requests must be answered without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receipt. This can be extended by two further months for complex or numerous requests, provided the person is told within the first month. Answering is free, unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive. If you have reasonable doubts about the person’s identity, you may ask for additional information, but not more than needed.

A good request process has a single entry point (a form or an address), a log of requests with dates, a procedure to verify identity proportionately, a map of where the data is stored so that nothing is forgotten, templates for answers, and a check before sending that the answer does not reveal other people’s data. Regulators often receive complaints about access requests that were ignored or answered late.

Cookies and similar trackers follow an additional rule from the ePrivacy directive (in France, article 82 of the Loi Informatique et Libertés): consent is required for non-essential cookies such as advertising and most analytics, and refusing must be as easy as accepting. The CNIL has fined large websites for making refusal harder than acceptance.
points: Privacy notice (articles 13-14): who, why, basis, recipients, transfers, retention, rights, right to complain.
Rights: access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, no solely automated significant decisions.
Answer within one month; extendable by two months for complex requests if the person is told within the first month.
Process: single entry point, request log, proportionate identity check, data map, templates, third-party data check.
Non-essential cookies need consent, and refusing must be as easy as accepting.

lessons.title: Accountability: the record, retention and the DPO
text: The record of processing activities (article 30) is the backbone of GDPR compliance. For each processing, the controller records: its name and contact details (and the DPO’s), the purposes, the categories of people and of data, the recipients, transfers outside the EU with their safeguards, the retention periods where possible, and a general description of the security measures. Processors keep their own, simpler record. The exemption for organisations under 250 employees is narrow in practice, so most organisations keep one.

Build the record by department: HR (recruitment, payroll, training), sales and marketing (customers, prospects, newsletter), IT (logs, access badges, CCTV), finance (suppliers, invoices). Interview each manager, list the tools they use, and fill one line per purpose. Then review it at least once a year and whenever a project or a tool changes.

Retention periods apply the storage limitation principle. Define them per purpose, often in two steps: an active period when the data is used, then archiving for legal reasons with restricted access, then deletion or anonymisation. Examples commonly used in France: unsuccessful job applicants up to 2 years after the last contact unless they agree to longer; customer data for commercial prospecting up to 3 years after the last contact; accounting documents 10 years; CCTV footage generally up to one month. Deletion must actually happen: plan it in the tools.

Data protection by design and by default (article 25) means building these rules into projects and systems: minimal data collected by default, privacy settings on the protective side, pseudonymisation where possible, retention automated, access limited. The GRC analyst checks this in project reviews, which is far cheaper than fixing a system after launch.

A data protection officer (DPO) is mandatory for public authorities, and for organisations whose core activities involve regular and systematic monitoring of people on a large scale or large-scale processing of special categories or criminal data. The DPO informs and advises, monitors compliance, advises on impact assessments and is the contact for the supervisory authority and for people. The DPO must be independent, involved early, have resources, and not be in a conflict of interest, which is why the head of IT or of marketing is usually not a suitable DPO.
points: Article 30 record: purposes, categories of people and data, recipients, transfers and safeguards, retention, security measures.
Build it department by department; review yearly and on every change.
Retention per purpose: active use → restricted archive → deletion or anonymisation, applied in the tools.
Privacy by design and by default (article 25): minimal data, protective settings, pseudonymisation, limited access.
DPO mandatory for public bodies, large-scale monitoring or large-scale sensitive data; independent, no conflict of interest.

example.code:
Record of processing (one line)
Processing        Recruitment
Purpose           Select candidates for open positions
Lawful basis      Pre-contractual steps (contract) / legitimate interests for the talent pool
People            Applicants
Data              Identity, contact, CV, cover letter, interview notes
Recipients        HR team, hiring managers; ATS provider (processor)
Transfers         None (ATS hosted in the EU)
Retention         Active until the decision; talent pool 2 years after last contact
Security          Access by role, MFA on the ATS, deletion automated
example.note: One line of the record for recruitment, with the information article 30 requires.

lessons.title: Data protection impact assessments
text: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA, AIPD in French, also called PIA) is required before a processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people’s rights and freedoms (article 35). The GDPR names three cases: systematic and extensive evaluation of people with significant effects, such as profiling for credit; large-scale processing of special categories or criminal data; and systematic monitoring of public areas on a large scale.

The European Data Protection Board’s guidelines list nine criteria: evaluation or scoring, automated decisions with significant effect, systematic monitoring, sensitive or highly personal data, large scale, matching or combining datasets, vulnerable people (employees, patients, children), innovative use of technology, and processing that prevents people from exercising a right or using a service. As a rule of thumb, a processing that meets two criteria needs a DPIA. Supervisory authorities also publish lists: the CNIL’s list includes, for example, health data processed by health institutions, large-scale employee monitoring and profiling for fraud detection.

A DPIA has four parts. Describe the processing: purposes, data, people, recipients, systems, retention, life cycle. Assess necessity and proportionality: lawful basis, minimisation, accuracy, retention, information and rights, processors, transfers. Assess the risks to people, typically three feared events: illegitimate access to data, unwanted modification and disappearance of data, each with its sources, threats, impacts on people, likelihood and severity. Plan the measures that reduce these risks and assess the residual risk.

The CNIL offers free PIA software that guides each step and produces a report. The DPO must be consulted, and the views of the people concerned or their representatives should be sought when appropriate, for example the works council for an employee monitoring tool. The DPIA is validated by the controller and kept, and it must be updated when the processing changes.

If the residual risk remains high despite the measures, the controller must consult the supervisory authority before starting (prior consultation, article 36). In practice this is rare: a good DPIA leads to measures that bring the risk down, or to a change in the project, for example collecting less data or giving people a real choice.
points: DPIA required for processing likely to result in a high risk (article 35), before it starts.
Nine EDPB criteria; two or more usually means a DPIA; the CNIL publishes a list of processing that requires one.
Four parts: description, necessity and proportionality, risks to people (illegitimate access, unwanted modification, disappearance), measures.
Consult the DPO; seek the views of people or their representatives where appropriate; update on change.
High residual risk → prior consultation of the supervisory authority (article 36).

example.code:
Project: badge and camera system to monitor access to a warehouse
EDPB criteria met
  [x] Systematic monitoring             [x] Vulnerable people (employees)
  [ ] Sensitive data                    [x] Innovative technology (face matching)
  [x] Large scale (900 staff, 24/7)     [ ] Automated decision
=> 4 criteria: DPIA required before deployment
Key measures: no face matching (badge only), cameras on entrances not workstations,
footage kept 30 days, access by security team only, staff and works council informed
example.note: Counting the criteria shows a DPIA is needed; the assessment then changes the project to reduce the risk.

lessons.title: Processors, contracts and transfers outside the EU
text: A controller may only use processors that provide sufficient guarantees, and must sign a contract with each one (article 28). The contract states the subject, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the types of data and people, and requires the processor to act only on documented instructions, keep the data confidential, ensure security (article 32), use sub-processors only with authorisation and the same obligations, help the controller with rights requests, security, breaches and DPIAs, delete or return the data at the end, and allow audits.

The GRC analyst checks these clauses in supplier contracts, often in a data processing agreement (DPA) annexed to the main contract, together with the security review: certifications, location of data, list of sub-processors and how the controller is told about changes. A processor that uses the data for its own purposes becomes a controller for that use, which must be identified and stopped or justified.

Transfers of personal data outside the European Economic Area are allowed only under the conditions of Chapter V. The simplest is an adequacy decision by the European Commission, recognising that a country protects data at a level essentially equivalent: for example the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Japan, and the United States for companies certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework since July 2023. Otherwise, appropriate safeguards are needed, mostly the Commission’s standard contractual clauses (SCCs), or binding corporate rules within a group. A few derogations (article 49), such as explicit consent, are for occasional cases only.

Since the Schrems II judgment of the Court of Justice of the EU in July 2020, which invalidated the previous Privacy Shield, an organisation relying on SCCs must also assess whether the law and practice of the destination country could prevent the clauses from being respected, in a transfer impact assessment, and add supplementary measures if needed, such as encryption with keys kept in the EU.

Transfers include remote access: a support team in a third country that can view EU customer data is a transfer, even if the data is stored in Europe. That is why reviewing a SaaS tool means asking where the data is hosted, where support and sub-processors are located, and which transfer mechanism covers each of them.
points: Article 28 contract: instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processors, assistance, deletion or return, audits.
Check the DPA, sub-processor list, data location and change notifications during supplier reviews.
Transfers outside the EEA: adequacy decision (UK, Switzerland, Japan, US companies under the Data Privacy Framework), or SCCs / binding corporate rules.
Schrems II (2020): transfer impact assessment and supplementary measures with SCCs.
Remote access from a third country is a transfer too.

example.code:
SaaS review: customer support tool
Hosting            EU (Frankfurt)                        OK
Sub-processors     12; support team in the Philippines   Transfer -> SCCs + TIA needed
                   AI features provider in the US        DPF certified? -> check list
DPA (art. 28)      Signed, audit right limited to        Ask for SOC 2 type II report
                   reports
Deletion at end    30 days after termination             OK
Security           ISO 27001 (scope covers the product)  OK
example.note: A processor review: hosting in the EU is not enough when support and sub-processors access the data from elsewhere.

lessons.title: Security and personal data breaches
text: Article 32 requires security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs and the nature of the processing: for example pseudonymisation and encryption, the ability to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, the ability to restore data in time after an incident, and regular testing of the measures. This is where GDPR meets ISO 27001: the same access controls, backups and logging serve both.

A personal data breach is a security incident leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of or access to personal data. It is not only hacking: an e-mail sent to the wrong recipients, a lost laptop that is not encrypted, ransomware that makes data unavailable, or an employee consulting files without reason are all breaches.

When a breach occurs, the controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people (article 33). If all the information is not available, a first notification can be completed later. If the breach is likely to result in a high risk, the people concerned must also be informed without undue delay, in clear language, with advice to protect themselves (article 34). A processor must inform the controller without undue delay.

Every breach, even one that is not notified, must be documented internally: facts, effects and remedial actions. Assess the risk with simple questions: what data (sensitive, financial, identity documents), how many people, can they be identified, was the data encrypted, was it really accessed, can the consequences be stopped? A misdirected e-mail with one ordinary address may not need notification; a lost unencrypted laptop with patient files certainly does.

Prepare before it happens: a breach procedure linked to the security incident process, a clear owner of the decision (usually the DPO advises and management decides), notification templates, contacts at the supervisory authority (in France, the CNIL’s online notification service), and a breach register. The 72 hours include weekends, so the procedure must work on a Saturday.
points: Article 32: security appropriate to the risk (encryption, pseudonymisation, resilience, restore, regular tests).
Breach: destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or access, accidental or unlawful.
Notify the authority within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless unlikely to result in a risk; complete later if needed.
High risk → inform the people concerned without undue delay, in clear language.
Document every breach in a register; prepare procedure, owner, templates and contacts in advance.

pitfalls: Using consent for everything, including employment, where it is rarely free.
Thinking pseudonymised data is anonymous: if a key exists, it is still personal data.
Keeping data “just in case” with no retention period, or defining periods that are never applied.
Answering rights requests late or forgetting systems where the data also lives.
Signing SaaS contracts without a data processing agreement or a look at sub-processors.
Ignoring remote access from outside the EU when assessing transfers.
Waiting for all the facts before notifying a breach: notify within 72 hours and complete later.

exercises.q: Sort these processing activities by their most suitable lawful basis.

groups.name: Legal obligation
items: Keeping invoices for the tax authorities

groups.name: Consent
items: Sending a marketing newsletter to prospects
Placing advertising cookies on a website

groups.name: Legitimate interests
items: Logging access to the IT systems for security

exercises.answer: Contract covers what is needed to deliver what the person signed up for; legal obligation covers what a law requires; consent fits optional uses such as newsletters to prospects and advertising cookies; legitimate interests fits security and fraud prevention, after a documented balancing test.

exercises.q: Match each right with a request that uses it.
pairs: “Send me a copy of all the data you hold about me.”
“My address is wrong in your system, please correct it.”
“I closed my account, delete my data.”
“Give me my order history in a file I can import elsewhere.”
exercises.answer: Each right has its own conditions: erasure does not cover data the law requires you to keep (invoices), objection to direct marketing is absolute, and portability covers data the person provided when processing relies on consent or contract and is automated.

exercises.q: A company uses a cloud HR tool to manage its staff. The tool provider only processes the data to run the service, following the company’s settings. What is the provider?
exercises.answer: The company decides why and how the HR data is processed: it is the controller. The provider acts on its instructions: it is a processor, and an article 28 contract is required. If the provider reused the data for its own purposes, such as training a product for other clients, it would become a controller for that use.

exercises.q: Within how many hours must a personal data breach be notified to the supervisory authority, when it is likely to result in a risk?
exercises.answer: 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach, without undue delay. If some information is missing, notify within 72 hours and complete later; if the notification is late, explain the reasons for the delay.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a breach response in order.
steps: Contain the incident (stop the leak, secure the systems)
Establish the facts: what data, how many people, encrypted or not
Assess the risk to the people concerned
Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours if there is a risk
Inform the people concerned if the risk is high
Record the breach and the lessons learned in the register
exercises.answer: Containment first, then facts, then risk assessment, which decides whether the authority (risk) and the people (high risk) are notified. Recording happens for every breach, notified or not, and lessons learned feed the security improvements.

exercises.q: In B3, compute the maximum fine for an infringement of the basic principles: the higher of 20 million euros and 4 % of worldwide annual turnover.
exercises.explain: 4 % of 900 million is 36 million, higher than 20 million, so the maximum is 36 million euros. For a company with 300 million of turnover, 4 % is 12 million and the 20 million ceiling applies. Real fines are set case by case and are usually far below the maximum.

exercises.q: A project team wants to deploy a tool that scores employees’ productivity from their computer activity, with automatic alerts to managers. Does it need a DPIA?
options: No, employee data is never sensitive
No, a DPIA is only for health data
Yes: it meets several criteria (evaluation or scoring, systematic monitoring, vulnerable people as employees, possibly innovative technology)
Only if employees give their consent
exercises.answer: Scoring, systematic monitoring and vulnerable people (employees, given the imbalance of power) are three of the nine criteria, so a DPIA is required before deployment, with the DPO consulted and staff representatives informed. The assessment may well conclude that such monitoring is disproportionate. Consent would not fix this, since it is rarely free in employment.

exercises.q: On Friday at 18:00, a sales employee reports that a spreadsheet with 3,000 customers’ names, e-mails and purchase history was sent by mistake to an external partner. Walk through your response.

choices.label: Contact the partner to ask for deletion and written confirmation, record the time you became aware, and open a breach file
choices.feedback: Right: contain first, and note the time because the 72 hours start when you became aware.

choices.label: Wait until Monday to discuss it with the DPO
choices.feedback: The 72 hours include the weekend: by Monday a third of the time is gone and the data may have spread.

choices.label: Delete the e-mail from the sender’s mailbox and close the matter
choices.feedback: Deleting your copy does not remove the partner’s copy, and you must keep a record of the breach.

steps.text: The partner confirms deletion on Saturday. Do you notify the CNIL?

choices.label: Assess the risk: 3,000 people, contact and purchase data, a known partner who confirmed deletion; likely a limited risk, so notify within 72 hours to be safe, and document the reasoning
choices.feedback: A sensible approach: the risk is reduced by the confirmation but not zero, so notifying within the deadline and documenting the analysis is defensible.

choices.label: No notification and no record, since it was deleted
choices.feedback: Even if you decide not to notify, every breach must be documented internally with the reasoning.

choices.label: Notify every customer immediately by SMS
choices.feedback: Informing people is required when the risk is high; here it is limited, and a rushed message could cause more worry than help.

choices.label: Record the breach and decision in the register, and fix the cause: data exports restricted, a sharing tool with access control instead of attachments, staff reminded
choices.feedback: Yes: the register keeps the accountability record, and the corrective actions prevent recurrence.

choices.label: Sanction the employee and change nothing else
choices.feedback: The error was human, but the process allowed a full customer export by e-mail; fix the process.

choices.label: Nothing, the incident is closed
choices.feedback: Without lessons learned, the same mistake will happen again.

exercises.answer: Contain, note the time of awareness, assess the risk with the facts, notify within 72 hours when there is a risk and inform people when it is high, document every decision in the breach register, and fix the cause.

exercises.q: Write one line of the record of processing activities for a gym’s membership management, including members’ health questionnaires.
exercises.hint: Purpose, basis (and article 9 exception), people, data, recipients, transfers, retention, security.
exercises.answer: Processing: membership management. Purposes: register members, manage subscriptions and payments, control access to the club, and check fitness to train. Lawful bases: contract for membership and payments; legal obligation for accounting; explicit consent under article 9 for the health questionnaire, which stays optional where the law allows. People: members. Data: identity, contact details, photo for the access card, subscription and payment data, access logs, health questionnaire answers. Recipients: reception and management staff, coaches for the health questionnaire only; processors: membership software provider and payment provider. Transfers: none, software hosted in the EU. Retention: membership data for the contract plus 3 years for prospecting, accounting records 10 years, access logs 3 months, health questionnaire deleted at the end of the membership. Security: access by role, health answers visible only to coaches, MFA on the software, encrypted backups.

exercises.q: A marketing manager wants to buy a list of 50,000 consumer e-mail addresses to send promotions. What do you advise?
exercises.answer: In France and most of the EU, sending marketing e-mails to consumers requires their prior consent, given to us or to a partner for named partners, unless they are existing customers receiving offers for similar products. A purchased list rarely meets this: I would ask the seller for proof of consent for each address (when, how, which wording, naming our company or a clearly defined category of partners) and the date of collection. Without proof, I advise against it: the risk is CNIL sanctions, complaints and harm to our sender reputation. I would propose alternatives: our own opt-in campaigns, partnerships where the partner sends the offer to its consenting customers, and offers to existing customers with an easy opt-out.

exercises.q: Your company plans to use an American AI service to summarise customer support tickets, which contain names, e-mails and sometimes order problems. What do you check?
exercises.answer: First the roles and the purpose: the service should be a processor acting on our instructions, with an article 28 data processing agreement that forbids using our data to train its models for others. Then the transfer: is the provider certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework for this service, or do we need SCCs with a transfer impact assessment, and can we choose EU hosting? Then minimisation: can we remove or pseudonymise names and e-mails before sending tickets, and limit the fields? Then security and retention at the provider: encryption, access, how long prompts and outputs are kept, deletion. I would check whether a DPIA is needed (innovative technology plus large scale may meet two criteria), update the record of processing and the privacy notice, and consult the DPO before launch.

interview.q: What is the difference between a controller and a processor?
interview.a: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and carries the main responsibility, including accountability. The processor processes the data on the controller’s behalf and only on its documented instructions, under an article 28 contract. A payroll software provider is a processor for the employer; if it reused the data for its own purposes, it would become a controller for that use.

interview.q: What are the lawful bases for processing personal data?
interview.a: Article 6 gives six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. The basis is chosen before processing and recorded. Consent is not always best: in employment it is rarely free, so HR processing usually relies on contract or legal obligation. Legitimate interests requires a documented balancing test against people’s rights.

Before any processing likely to result in a high risk to people’s rights and freedoms. The GDPR names profiling with significant effects, large-scale sensitive data and large-scale monitoring of public areas; the EDPB lists nine criteria, and meeting two usually means a DPIA is needed. National authorities like the CNIL publish lists too. The DPIA describes the processing, checks necessity and proportionality, assesses the risks to people and defines measures; if the residual risk stays high, the authority must be consulted.

interview.q: A customer asks for all their data. How do you handle it?
interview.a: I log the request with its date, check the person’s identity proportionately, search every system where their data lives using the record of processing as a map, and prepare a copy with the information required: purposes, recipients, retention, rights and source. Before sending, I remove other people’s data. The answer goes out within one month; if the request is complex, I tell the person within that month that we will need up to two more months.

interview.q: What do you do in the first 72 hours of a personal data breach?
interview.a: Contain it, note when we became aware, gather the facts: what data, how many people, whether it was encrypted and really accessed. Assess the risk to the people. If there is a risk, notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours, even with incomplete information to be completed later. If the risk is high, inform the people concerned in clear language with advice. Record everything in the breach register, including decisions not to notify, and then fix the cause.

interview.q: How can personal data be transferred to the United States?
interview.a: Through an adequacy decision: since July 2023, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework covers transfers to American companies that are certified under it. Otherwise, with appropriate safeguards, mostly the standard contractual clauses, plus a transfer impact assessment and supplementary measures if needed, as required since the Schrems II judgment. Remote access from the US to data stored in Europe is a transfer too, so I check support and sub-processors as well as hosting.

interview.q: How do GDPR and ISO 27001 work together?
interview.a: GDPR article 32 requires security appropriate to the risk, and an ISO 27001 ISMS provides the structured way to deliver it: access control, encryption, backups, logging, supplier management and incident response serve both. ISO 27701 extends ISO 27001 with privacy controls. But GDPR goes beyond security: lawful bases, minimisation, retention, rights, transparency and transfers are not covered by ISO 27001, so a company can be certified and still not be GDPR compliant.
